abstract: |
  This brief report compares the local Large, Mid and Small Cap indexes with the Capped SWIX benchmark since 2015, using monthly constituent weights and daily stock returns. Large Caps are close to the benchmark (an active share of only 13% today), but their sector mix has swung from Industrials to Resources, leaving them highly exposed to the rand and to bad news. Small Caps hold the most volatile stocks, yet form the least volatile index in every year, because their stocks move largely independently; the price is the deepest drawdown in the sample. Mid Caps have the weakest long-run return, but they are the only index that held up in periods of local market and currency stress. Size, in other words, is mainly a bet on sectors and on the rand.

```{r functions, include=FALSE}
# All functions used in this report (the same functions as in the code/ folder),
# defined here so the document knits on its own.

# Annualised realised volatility per calendar year, one column per series
# df: tidy frame with columns date, Name, Return (daily simple returns)
Vol_Table <- function(df, Scale = 252) {

  df %>%
    mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
    group_by(Year, Name) %>%
    summarise(Vol = sd(Return, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(Scale), .groups = "drop") %>%
    spread(Name, Vol)

}

# Rolling annualised volatility plot
# df: tidy frame with columns date, Name, Return (daily simple returns)
Roll_Vol_Plot <- function(df, Width = 63, Scale = 252, Title = "", Subtitle = "") {

  df_plot <-
    df %>%
    group_by(Name) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(RollVol = RcppRoll::roll_sd(Return, n = Width, fill = NA, align = "right") * sqrt(Scale)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!is.na(RollVol))

  g <-
    df_plot %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_line(aes(date, RollVol, color = Name), alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.8) +
    labs(title = Title, subtitle = Subtitle, x = "", y = "Annualised volatility") +
    fmxdat::theme_fmx(title.size = fmxdat::ggpts(30), subtitle.size = fmxdat::ggpts(25),
                      legend.size = fmxdat::ggpts(25), axis.size = fmxdat::ggpts(25))

  fmxdat::finplot(g, y.pct = TRUE, y.pct_acc = 1, x.date.type = "%Y", x.date.dist = "1 year")

}

# Fit an AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) to one return series and return the fit
# Return: xts of demeaned daily log returns (one column)
GARCH_Fit <- function(Return, Model = "gjrGARCH", Dist = "sstd") {

  spec <- rugarch::ugarchspec(
    variance.model = list(model = Model, garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
    mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(1, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
    distribution.model = Dist)

  rugarch::ugarchfit(spec = spec, data = Return, solver = "hybrid")

}

# Compare the four GARCH variants used in Prac 6 on information criteria
GARCH_Compare <- function(Return, Dist = "sstd") {

  Models <- c("sGARCH", "gjrGARCH", "eGARCH", "apARCH")
  model.list <- list()
  for (p in seq_along(Models)) {
    model.list[[p]] <- GARCH_Fit(Return, Model = Models[p], Dist = Dist)
  }
  fit.mat <- sapply(model.list, rugarch::infocriteria)
  colnames(fit.mat) <- Models
  rownames(fit.mat) <- rownames(rugarch::infocriteria(model.list[[1]]))
  fit.mat

}

# Extract annualised conditional volatility from a fit as a tidy frame
GARCH_Sigma <- function(Fit, Name, Scale = 252) {

  rugarch::sigma(Fit) %>%
    tbl2xts::xts_tbl() %>%
    setNames(c("date", "Sigma")) %>%
    mutate(date = as.Date(date), Sigma = Sigma * sqrt(Scale), Name = Name)

}

# Fill missing sector labels: first from the same stock's other months,
# then from the daily index constituents and SafeCore holdings; the rest = "Unclassified"
Fill_Sectors <- function(Size_Idx, Index_Constituents, SafeCore) {

  Lookup <-
    bind_rows(
      Size_Idx %>% filter(!is.na(Sector)) %>% select(Tickers, Sector),
      Index_Constituents %>% filter(SuperSector != "") %>% select(Tickers, Sector = SuperSector),
      SafeCore %>% filter(!is.na(Sector)) %>% select(Tickers, Sector)) %>%
    count(Tickers, Sector) %>%
    group_by(Tickers) %>% filter(n == max(n)) %>% slice(1) %>% ungroup() %>%
    select(Tickers, Sector_Fill = Sector)

  Size_Idx %>%
    left_join(Lookup, by = "Tickers") %>%
    mutate(Sector = coalesce(Sector, Sector_Fill, "Unclassified")) %>%
    select(-Sector_Fill)

}

# Daily returns of each size index rebuilt from monthly weights and daily stock returns
# (Safe_Return.portfolio: month-end weights applied from the next trading day)
Size_Index_Returns <- function(Size_Idx, Stock_Rets, StartDate) {

  Funds <- unique(Size_Idx$Fund)
  Out <- list()

  for (f in Funds) {

    W_xts <-
      Size_Idx %>% filter(Fund == f, date >= StartDate) %>%
      select(date, Tickers, Weight) %>%
      tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Weight, spread_by = Tickers)
    W_xts[is.na(W_xts)] <- 0

    R_xts <-
      Stock_Rets %>% filter(Tickers %in% colnames(W_xts), date > StartDate) %>%
      tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Return, spread_by = Tickers)
    R_xts[is.na(R_xts)] <- 0

    W_xts <- W_xts[, colnames(R_xts)]                       # stocks without return data dropped
    W_xts <- W_xts / rowSums(W_xts)                          # re-normalise to 100%

    Port <- rmsfuns::Safe_Return.portfolio(R = R_xts, weights = W_xts, lag_weights = TRUE,
                                           verbose = TRUE, value = 1, geometric = TRUE)

    Out[[f]] <- Port$returns %>% xts_tbl() %>% setNames(c("date", "Return")) %>%
      mutate(date = as.Date(date), Name = f)
  }

  bind_rows(Out)

}

# Stock concentration per index and month:
# number of stocks, weight of the 10 largest, Herfindahl index and effective number of stocks (1 / HHI)
Concentration <- function(Size_Idx) {

  Size_Idx %>%
    group_by(Fund, date) %>%
    mutate(w = Weight / sum(Weight)) %>%
    summarise(N_Stocks = n(),
              Top10 = sum(sort(w, decreasing = TRUE)[1:min(10, n())]),
              HHI = sum(w^2),
              Eff_N = 1 / HHI, .groups = "drop")

}

# Active share of each index relative to a benchmark index, per month:
# AS = 0.5 * sum_i | w_i(index) - w_i(benchmark) |, stocks missing from one side get weight 0
Active_Share <- function(Size_Idx, Bench = "CappedSWIX") {

  W <- Size_Idx %>% group_by(Fund, date) %>% mutate(w = Weight / sum(Weight)) %>% ungroup()
  B <- W %>% filter(Fund == Bench) %>% select(date, Tickers, w_B = w)

  W %>%
    filter(Fund != Bench) %>%
    select(Fund, date, Tickers, w) %>%
    group_by(Fund) %>%
    group_modify(~ full_join(.x, B %>% filter(date %in% .x$date), by = c("date", "Tickers"))) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(w = coalesce(w, 0), w_B = coalesce(w_B, 0)) %>%
    group_by(Fund, date) %>%
    summarise(Active_Share = 0.5 * sum(abs(w - w_B)), .groups = "drop")

}

# Rolling annualised returns from daily returns (Prac 1: RcppRoll::roll_prod)
Roll_Returns <- function(df, Years = 3, Scale = 252) {

  df %>%
    group_by(Name) %>% arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(RollRet = RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Return, n = Years * Scale, fill = NA, align = "right")^(1 / Years) - 1) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!is.na(RollRet))

}

# Stratification: annualised return and volatility of each index in the selected months,
# against its full-sample values (Prac 2 Bonus idea, extended to returns)
# Idxs: tidy (date, YearMonth, Name, Return) of winsorised daily returns
Strat_Perf <- function(Idxs, YMs, Alias, Scale = 252) {

  Full <- Idxs %>% group_by(Name) %>%
    summarise(Full_Ret = mean(Return) * Scale, Full_SD = sd(Return) * sqrt(Scale), .groups = "drop")

  Idxs %>% filter(YearMonth %in% YMs) %>%
    group_by(Name) %>%
    summarise(Ret = mean(Return) * Scale, SD = sd(Return) * sqrt(Scale), .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(Full, by = "Name") %>%
    mutate(SD_Ratio = SD / Full_SD, Period = Alias)

}

# Realised volatility of constituents vs the index itself at a date (trailing year):
# weighted-average stock volatility, median stock volatility, index volatility,
# and the diversification ratio = weighted-average stock vol / index vol
Constituent_Vol <- function(RebDate, Size_Idx, Stock_Rets, Index_Rets, LookBack = 252) {

  W <- Size_Idx %>% filter(date == RebDate) %>% group_by(Fund) %>% mutate(w = Weight / sum(Weight)) %>% ungroup()

  Stock_Vol <-
    Stock_Rets %>%
    filter(Tickers %in% W$Tickers, date <= RebDate, date > RebDate - 2 * LookBack) %>%
    group_by(Tickers) %>% filter(row_number() > n() - LookBack) %>%
    summarise(Vol = sd(Return, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(252), N = sum(!is.na(Return)), .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(N > LookBack / 2)

  Idx_Vol <-
    Index_Rets %>% filter(date <= RebDate) %>%
    group_by(Name) %>% filter(row_number() > n() - LookBack) %>%
    summarise(Index_Vol = sd(Return) * sqrt(252), .groups = "drop")

  W %>% inner_join(Stock_Vol, by = "Tickers") %>%
    group_by(Fund) %>%
    summarise(Wtd_Stock_Vol = sum(w * Vol) / sum(w), Median_Stock_Vol = median(Vol), .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(Idx_Vol, by = c("Fund" = "Name")) %>%
    mutate(Div_Ratio = Wtd_Stock_Vol / Index_Vol, date = RebDate)

}
```

# Introduction \label{Introduction}

Investors often treat size as a simple risk dial: small caps are risky, large caps are safe. This report tests that view for the local market. Using the monthly constituents of the Large, Mid and Small Cap indexes, and the Capped SWIX as the benchmark, we compare their sector exposures, stock concentration, volatility and returns since 2015. We use four techniques: realised volatility (including a GARCH model), rolling returns, active share and stratification by market regime. The short answer is that size is mainly a bet on sectors and on the rand, and that the "safest" looking index carries hidden tail risk.

# Data and Methodology \label{Data}

Monthly constituent weights for the four indexes run from 2007, and daily stock returns from 2015, so our analysis starts in January 2015. Each index's daily return is rebuilt from its month-end weights, applied from the next trading day. The rebuilt indexes track the official ones closely, with correlations of 0.98 to 0.99. Daily stock returns beyond $\pm 50\%$ are treated as data errors, and weights are rescaled to 100%. Missing sector labels are filled from the other datasets; about 8% of Small Cap weight before 2020 remains unclassified.

**Concentration** is measured by the weight in the ten largest stocks and by the effective number of stocks, $N^{eff} = 1/\sum_i w_i^2$: the number of equally weighted stocks that would give the same concentration. **Realised volatility** is $\sqrt{252}\,sd(r_t)$, per calendar year and on a rolling 63-day window, and we also fit a GJR-GARCH(1,1) model to each index [@glosten1993]. To compare constituents with their index we use the diversification ratio,

\begin{align}
DR_t = \frac{\sum_i w_{i,t}\, \sigma_{i,t}}{\sigma_{index,t}}, \label{eq1}
\end{align}

which is high when stocks are volatile on their own but move independently. **Rolling returns** are annualised three-year returns. **Active share** measures how different each index's holdings are from the benchmark [@cremers2009]:

\begin{align}
AS_t = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \left| w_{i,t}^{index} - w_{i,t}^{SWIX} \right|, \label{eq2}
\end{align}

where 0 means identical holdings and 1 means no overlap. Finally, **stratification** compares each index's return and volatility in the months that fall in the top (bottom) 20% of local market volatility, rand volatility and the VIX.

# Results \label{Results}

## Risk and return

```{r tab1, results = 'asis'}
Size_xts <- Size_Rets %>% mutate(Name = gsub(" ", "_", Name)) %>% tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = Return, spread_by = Name)
Risk_Tab <- rbind(table.AnnualizedReturns(Size_xts, scale = 252),
                  ES(Size_xts, p = 0.95, method = "modified"),
                  maxDrawdown(Size_xts))
data.frame(Measure = c("Annualised return", "Annualised volatility", "Sharpe ratio (Rf = 0)",
                       "Modified ES (95%, daily)", "Maximum drawdown"), Risk_Tab, check.names = FALSE) %>%
  select(Measure, `Capped SWIX` = Capped_SWIX, `Large Caps` = Large_Caps, `Mid Caps` = Mid_Caps, `Small Caps` = Small_Caps) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Risk and return, January 2015 to September 2026 \\label{tab1}", Digits = 3)
```

Table \ref{tab1} already challenges the simple view of size. Small Caps have the lowest volatility (13.5%) and the best Sharpe ratio, and Large Caps the highest volatility. Mid Caps have the weakest return. But Small Caps also suffered by far the deepest drawdown (50%, during COVID): their low daily volatility hides a crash risk that only shows up in extreme markets. Part of this is a liquidity effect, as thinly traded stocks are priced less often, which smooths measured daily volatility.

## Sector exposure and concentration

```{r Figure1, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Sector exposure of the size indexes \\label{Figure1}", fig.height = 4.2, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
Sector_Exp <- Size_Idx %>% group_by(Fund, date, Sector) %>% summarise(Weight = sum(Weight), .groups = "drop")
g <- Sector_Exp %>% filter(date >= ymd(20150101)) %>%
  ggplot() + geom_area(aes(date, Weight, fill = Sector), position = "stack") +
  facet_wrap(~Fund) + labs(x = "", y = "") + fmxdat::theme_fmx()
fmxdat::finplot(g, y.pct = TRUE, x.date.type = "%y", x.date.dist = "2 years")
```

```{r tab2, results = 'asis'}
Rand_Exp <- Size_Idx %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>%
  left_join(Hedge %>% select(Tickers, hedge), by = "Tickers") %>%
  mutate(hedge = ifelse(is.na(hedge) | hedge == "", "Not classified", hedge)) %>%
  group_by(Fund, hedge) %>% summarise(Weight = sum(Weight) * 100, .groups = "drop") %>%
  spread(hedge, Weight)
Conc <- Concentration(Size_Idx)
Conc %>% filter(date %in% c(ymd(20151231), ymd(20260831))) %>%
  mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
  select(Fund, Year, Top10, Eff_N) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = c(Top10, Eff_N)) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("Top10"), ~ . * 100)) %>%
  left_join(Rand_Exp %>% select(Fund, `Pure Rand Hedge`, `Rand Leverage`, `Rand Play`, `Rand Neutral`), by = "Fund") %>%
  setNames(c("Index", "Top10 2015", "Top10 2026", "Eff.N 2015", "Eff.N 2026",
             "Hedge", "Leverage", "Play", "Neutral")) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Concentration: weight in top 10 stocks (\\%) and effective number of stocks, December 2015 and August 2026; rand exposure (\\% of weight in pure rand hedges, rand-leveraged, rand-play and rand-neutral stocks), August 2026 \\label{tab2}", Digits = 1, Size = "\\scriptsize")
```

Figure \ref{Figure1} shows that the three indexes are very different portfolios. Large Caps have swung from Industrials (65% in 2015, much of it Naspers) to Resources (38% in 2026), and Table \ref{tab2} shows that almost 60% of their weight is now in rand hedges or rand-leveraged stocks. Mid Caps have shifted towards Financials, while Small Caps have become a Property and Industrials index (31% and 49%), with little exposure to the rand.

Concentration has moved in opposite directions. Large Caps became much less concentrated in 2023, when their effective number of stocks rose from about 12 to over 20, consistent with a cap on the largest stock's weight. Mid Caps, by contrast, have become more concentrated (their effective number fell from 38 to 25), so their risk now rests on fewer names.

## Realised volatility of the indexes and their constituents

```{r Figure2, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Rolling three-month realised volatility \\label{Figure2}", fig.height = 3.3, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
Roll_Vol_Plot(Size_Rets, Width = 63)
```

```{r vol_prep, include=FALSE}
Dec_Dates <- Size_Idx %>% distinct(date) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20151231), format(date, "%m") == "12" | date == max(date)) %>% pull(date)
CV <- map_df(Dec_Dates, ~ Constituent_Vol(.x, Size_Idx, Stock_Rets, Size_Rets))

xts_G <- Size_Rets %>% mutate(Name = gsub(" ", "_", Name)) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>% mutate(scaledret = log(1 + Return) - mean(log(1 + Return))) %>% ungroup() %>%
  tbl_xts(cols_to_xts = scaledret, spread_by = Name)
GARCH_Coefs <- map_df(colnames(xts_G), function(nm) {
  fit <- GARCH_Fit(na.omit(xts_G[, nm]))
  tibble(Index = gsub("_", " ", nm), alpha = coef(fit)["alpha1"], beta = coef(fit)["beta1"],
         gamma = coef(fit)["gamma1"], Persistence = persistence(fit))
})
```

```{r tab3, results = 'asis'}
CV %>% group_by(Fund) %>%
  summarise(`Avg stock vol` = mean(Wtd_Stock_Vol) * 100, `Index vol` = mean(Index_Vol) * 100,
            `Div. ratio (avg)` = mean(Div_Ratio), `Div. ratio (2026)` = Div_Ratio[date == max(date)]) %>%
  left_join(GARCH_Coefs, by = c("Fund" = "Index")) %>%
  rename(Index = Fund, `Stock vol` = `Avg stock vol`, `DR avg` = `Div. ratio (avg)`, `DR 2026` = `Div. ratio (2026)`,
         `$\\alpha$` = alpha, `$\\beta$` = beta, `$\\gamma$` = gamma) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Weighted average constituent volatility and index volatility (annual averages, \\%), diversification ratio (DR), and GJR-GARCH(1,1) estimates \\label{tab3}", Digits = 2, Size = "\\scriptsize")
```

Figure \ref{Figure2} shows that Small Caps are the least volatile index throughout, while Large Caps are usually the most volatile; in 2026 the gap is wide (12% against 22%). Table \ref{tab3} explains why. The stocks inside the Small Cap index are individually the most volatile, but they move largely independently, so their risks cancel out: the diversification ratio averages about 3, against about 2 for Large Caps. Large Cap stocks, by contrast, share common drivers such as commodity prices and the rand, so their risks add up.

The GARCH estimates add a second difference. Volatility is highly persistent in all four indexes (around 0.95), but the leverage effect, $\gamma$, is about twice as strong in Large Caps as in Small Caps. Bad news therefore raises volatility much more in the large-cap end of the market, which is where global shocks arrive first.

## Rolling returns and active share

```{r Figure3, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Rolling three-year annualised returns \\label{Figure3}", fig.height = 3.3, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
RR <- Roll_Returns(Size_Rets, Years = 3)
Beat <- RR %>% select(date, Name, RollRet) %>% spread(Name, RollRet) %>%
  summarise(across(c(`Large Caps`, `Mid Caps`, `Small Caps`), ~ mean(. > `Capped SWIX`)))
g <- RR %>% ggplot() + geom_line(aes(date, RollRet, color = Name), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + labs(x = "", y = "") + fmxdat::theme_fmx()
fmxdat::finplot(g, y.pct = TRUE, x.date.type = "%Y", x.date.dist = "1 year")
```

Figure \ref{Figure3} shows that Small Caps give the widest range of outcomes, from a three-year return of -20% after COVID to +43% in the recovery, with the highest median (16%). Large Caps beat the Capped SWIX over `r round(Beat[["Large Caps"]] * 100)`% of three-year windows, Small Caps over `r round(Beat[["Small Caps"]] * 100)`%, and Mid Caps over only `r round(Beat[["Mid Caps"]] * 100)`%.

```{r Figure4, fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = "Active share relative to the Capped SWIX \\label{Figure4}", fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6.5, dev = 'png'}
AS <- Active_Share(Size_Idx, Bench = "Capped SWIX")
g <- AS %>% filter(date >= ymd(20150101)) %>%
  ggplot() + geom_line(aes(date, Active_Share, color = Fund), linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "", y = "") + fmxdat::theme_fmx()
fmxdat::finplot(g, y.pct = TRUE, x.date.type = "%Y", x.date.dist = "1 year")
```

Active share in Figure \ref{Figure4} confirms how different the indexes are from the benchmark. Large Caps have an active share of only 13% today (25% on average), so they add very little to a portfolio that already holds the Capped SWIX. Mid Caps (around 80%) and Small Caps (around 95%) are genuinely different portfolios, and so offer real diversification away from the benchmark's dominant stocks.

## Stratification: behaviour in stressed regimes

```{r tab4, results = 'asis'}
Winsor <- function(x) { q <- quantile(x, c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE); pmin(pmax(x, q[1]), q[2]) }
Idxs <- Size_Rets %>% group_by(Name) %>% mutate(Return = Winsor(Return)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m"))
Monthly_Lvl <- function(df, Nm) df %>% filter(Name == Nm, date >= ymd(20150101)) %>%
  mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>% group_by(YearMonth) %>% summarise(Level = mean(TRI))
ZAR_M <- Local_Cncy_Vol_Index %>% mutate(Name = "SAVIUSD") %>% Monthly_Lvl("SAVIUSD")
VIX_M <- Monthly_Lvl(Implied_Vol, "VIX")
SWIXVol_M <- Size_Rets %>% filter(Name == "Capped SWIX") %>% mutate(YearMonth = format(date, "%Y%m")) %>%
  group_by(YearMonth) %>% summarise(Level = sd(Return) * sqrt(252))
Top_Q <- function(df) df %>% filter(Level > quantile(Level, 0.8)) %>% pull(YearMonth)
Bot_Q <- function(df) df %>% filter(Level < quantile(Level, 0.2)) %>% pull(YearMonth)
bind_rows(
  Strat_Perf(Idxs, Top_Q(SWIXVol_M), "High local vol"), Strat_Perf(Idxs, Bot_Q(SWIXVol_M), "Low local vol"),
  Strat_Perf(Idxs, Top_Q(ZAR_M), "High ZAR vol"),       Strat_Perf(Idxs, Bot_Q(ZAR_M), "Low ZAR vol"),
  Strat_Perf(Idxs, Top_Q(VIX_M), "High VIX"),           Strat_Perf(Idxs, Bot_Q(VIX_M), "Low VIX")) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Ret * 100) %>%
  select(Period, Name, Ret, SD_Ratio) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Name, values_from = c(Ret, SD_Ratio)) %>%
  select(Period, `Ret_Capped SWIX`, `Ret_Large Caps`, `Ret_Mid Caps`, `Ret_Small Caps`,
         `SD_Ratio_Capped SWIX`, `SD_Ratio_Large Caps`, `SD_Ratio_Mid Caps`, `SD_Ratio_Small Caps`) %>%
  setNames(c("Regime", "R: SWIX", "R: Large", "R: Mid", "R: Small",
             "V: SWIX", "V: Large", "V: Mid", "V: Small")) %>%
  Print_Table(Caption = "Annualised return (R, \\%) and volatility relative to the full sample (V), by regime \\label{tab4}", Digits = 2, Size = "\\scriptsize")
```

Table \ref{tab4} shows how the indexes behave when conditions change. In months of high local market volatility, Large Caps lost 3.9% a year while Mid Caps still gained 8.5%. In months of high rand volatility the gap is similar: Mid Caps returned 13.9%, against about 5% for Large and Small Caps. When the rand is calm, Large Caps do best. Mid Caps therefore act as a domestic hedge against local and currency stress, while Large Caps carry the rand and commodity risk of the benchmark. All indexes are about a third more volatile in stressed months, so stratification shows differences in returns rather than in the level of volatility. High-VIX months include strong rebound months, which explains their positive average returns.

# Conclusion \label{Conclusion}

Size is not a simple risk dial on the local market. Large Caps are close to the benchmark, but they have become a concentrated bet on Resources and on the rand, with the highest volatility and the strongest response to bad news. Small Caps look safest on daily volatility because their stocks move independently, but they suffered the deepest drawdown, so their risk lies in the tail. Mid Caps have the weakest long-run return, yet they are the only index that held up in local and currency stress. For a portfolio benchmarked to the Capped SWIX, Large Caps add little, while Mid and Small Caps offer genuine diversification, but each brings its own sector and liquidity risks that must be managed.
